items.title: Show HN: Flowfile – Open-source visual ETL that round-trips to Python (Polars)
items.summary: Hi HN, I'm Edward, the author of Flowfile. Flowfile is a visual ETL tool built on Polars. You build pipelines on a canvas, and every flow is also Python code. You can export it or write code with the FlowFrame API (Polars-like) and it shows up as a visual graph (or vice versa - keep reading). Flowfile is what it is today because I believe we are spending too much time translating non-technical and technical implementations of data problems. Sometimes visual works better, and sometimes code. You should be able to choose whichever is easiest, without fully committing to one way of working. Flowfile solves this by standardizing the backend component without favoring either visual or code. Which brings me to Flowfile's newest feature: notebook mode. The flow opens as Python cells that stay in sync with the canvas. If you add a filter (df.filter(...)) in a cell, it appears on the canvas. And it also works the other way around: if you add a sort on the canvas, it appears as a .sort(...) in the notebook. So now you can switch between visual and code without making a total mess of it under the hood. It also has a data catalog, a scheduler, sandboxed Python execution, etc.. It's MIT licensed, and `pip install flowfile` installs all dependencies. Github: https://github.com/edwardvaneechoud/Flowfile I'd love feedback, especially on the notebook mode.

items.title: Show HN: Termcraft – 2D terminal survival with multiplayer support
items.summary: Earlier this year, I started developing Termcraft, a terminal-based 2D survival game written in Rust. Since its first release more than half a year ago, I've added multiplayer support, so you can now host a game and play with friends (or colleagues during a meeting?); Up to 8 players. I've also substantially improved the visuals, lighting, physics, and overall gameplay. A friend and I ended up spending the entire weekend playing through the game from start to finish. The progression takes you from gathering wood and building a shelter to crafting equipment, exploring caves, finding diamonds, crossing the Nether, and fighting the Ender Dragon. There are villages, farming, collaborative building, PvP, and player chat along the way. It's open source under the AGPL-3.0 license, with downloadable builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Gameplay demo video: https://youtu.be/nn37_15dLFM Installation and controls: https://pagel-s.github.io/termcraft/ It's not perfect, but I'd love to hear your feedback and experiences with the game. Contributions are also more than welcome!

items.title: After LiteLLM's backdoor, we open-sourced an OS-level package firewall
Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
items.summary: Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself. Main features: - Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows) - Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.) - Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG) - MCP support - Image recognition - CRUD to your local filesystem - Works fully offline with no internet Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs. The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business. I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model. The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models). I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model. Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

items.title: Show HN: Ranwhat.com
items.summary: Hi HackerNews, My name is Matija, and I'm building ranwhat.com. It's used for checking if any of your secrets have leaked, and where they leaked. It's mostly aimed at solo devs such as myself, but also at anyone using a coding agent. The tool also checks if your coding agent ran any sketchy commands. This is mostly a "better safe than sorry" feature, so you can tell your Claude or Codex not to run them. The project is open source (MIT) and everything runs locally on your machine. How to install it: pip install ranwhat / uv tool install ranwhat, or brew install MatijaMiki/ranwhat/ranwhat There is a free and a paid plan. Everything local is free; the paid plan is 12€ a month and adds server-side features, which you can read more about here: https://ranwhat.com/pricing All I'm asking for here is feedback, and if you have anything you would want added to the project. Looking forward to answering any questions you have. Best, Matija

items.title: Show HN: Sóþspell, a model-guided walkthrough of a codebase
items.summary: I kept finding myself wanting a way to get talked through the code that a model had created, which led to me making Sóþspell (old English, "Truth Story"). You give it a git repo locally or via URL, and it creates a tour of the repo in a web page, with the aim of it explaining the whole thing. There's also model harness plugins for Claude, Codex, and OpenCode. You give it an API key for whatever model you prefer to create the tour (saved locally or via github), and you can also give it a voice using an ElevenLabs API key. I just pushed a canvas view, which I'm hoping I can make the code navigation a bit more helpful. There's a demo codebase, and you can export tours as JSON. The demo doesn't need any keys to work, it falls back to browser speech if you want to hear that. This is my first real, "big" open source project that I've released, prior to this I'd just contributed stuff. I hope it can be useful to someone! I would love to hear some constructive criticism too, and any suggestions on features you'd like to see. It's MIT licensed, and I'll try to stick around in the comments to answer questions if people want.
